subsections.subsection_title: HOW TO REPORT A NORMAL PROGRESS ASSESSMENT

blocks.text: “The woman is clinically stable and afebrile. The fetus is cephalic with a reassuring fetal heart rate. Contractions are approximately 3–4 in 10 minutes and of adequate duration. Vaginal examination shows progressive cervical dilatation with descent of the presenting part, no significant caput or moulding, and no evidence of malpresentation or obstruction. Labour appears to be progressing appropriately.”

subsections.subsection_title: REPORT — PROLONGED LABOUR FROM INADEQUATE POWER

blocks.text: “The woman is clinically stable and the fetal assessment is reassuring. Vaginal examination shows slow cervical progress, but there is no significant caput or moulding and the presenting part is appropriately positioned and descending. Uterine contractions are infrequent and of inadequate duration, suggesting inadequate uterine activity. I would assess for reversible causes and, if there is no evidence of obstruction and it is clinically appropriate, consider oxytocin augmentation with appropriate fetal monitoring.”

“The woman has poor cervical progress despite strong, frequent contractions. The fetal head remains high with minimal descent and there is significant caput and moulding. This is concerning for mechanical obstruction, possibly due to cephalopelvic disproportion or malposition. I would stop further augmentation, call for senior obstetric review, assess maternal and fetal wellbeing and plan delivery, most likely Caesarean birth if vaginal delivery is not safely achievable.”

“Vaginal examination demonstrates a cephalic presentation in persistent occipito-posterior position with slow descent. There is no significant fetal compromise. content_groups.group_title: Q1. What are the causes of prolonged labour?

blocks.text: “The causes can be remembered using the 3 Ps: abnormal power, abnormal passenger and abnormal passage.”

content_groups.group_title: Q2. What are the signs of obstructed labour?

blocks.text: “Poor or absent descent despite contractions, progressive caput and moulding, poor cervical progress, maternal exhaustion, dehydration, tachycardia, bladder dysfunction, fetal compromise and, in advanced cases, a pathological retraction ring or uterine rupture.”

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What is the difference between caput and moulding?

blocks.text: “Caput is oedema of the fetal scalp, whereas moulding is overlapping of the fetal skull bones.”

content_groups.group_title: Q4. What does severe moulding suggest?

blocks.text: “It raises concern for mechanical obstruction, particularly when associated with poor descent and strong contractions.”

content_groups.group_title: Q5. Should you augment every woman with slow labour?

blocks.text: “No. I would first assess the cause of poor progress and exclude malpresentation, malposition and mechanical obstruction before considering augmentation.”
“A mismatch between the fetal presenting part and the maternal pelvis such that safe vaginal passage is difficult or impossible.”

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What is the danger of giving oxytocin in obstructed labour?

blocks.text: “It can increase uterine activity against a mechanical obstruction, causing hyperstimulation, fetal compromise and potentially uterine rupture.”

content_groups.group_title: Q9. What is the management of obstructed labour?

blocks.text: “Stop augmentation, call senior help, stabilize the mother, assess the fetus, identify the cause and expedite delivery by the safest route. Caesarean birth is usually required when vaginal delivery is not safely achievable.”

content_groups.group_title: Q10. Can prolonged labour be diagnosed solely from the number of hours?

blocks.text: “No. Modern management considers cervical change, descent, contractions and maternal and fetal wellbeing rather than relying on a single rigid time threshold.”

items: “How would you assess and manage prolonged labour?”

blocks.text: “I would first assess the mother and fetus and establish which stage of labour she is in. I would review the contraction pattern, cervical dilatation and effacement, descent, fetal presentation and position, station, caput and moulding. I would assess maternal vital signs, hydration, pain, bleeding and temperature, and assess fetal wellbeing with appropriate monitoring.

I would use the 3 Ps framework: power, passenger and passage. I would determine whether the problem is inadequate uterine activity, fetal malpresentation or malposition, fetal size, or mechanical pelvic obstruction.

If contractions are inadequate and there is no evidence of obstruction, I would consider appropriate augmentation with oxytocin and monitor the mother and fetus closely. If there are strong contractions with poor descent, severe moulding or caput, I would suspect obstruction, stop further augmentation, call the senior obstetric team, stabilize the mother and plan delivery by the safest route.
If there is fetal compromise, maternal deterioration, infection or suspected uterine rupture, I would expedite delivery without unnecessary delay.”
That single sentence is one of the most valuable points in this station.
